title: Phenomenology
summary: Husserl proposed studying experience exactly as it is given. Each act of consciousness (noesis) is directed at an object as it is meant (noema), and philosophy should 'bracket' the taken-for-granted existence of the outside world (epoché) to describe how things appear.

title: Hilbert's programme
summary: Hilbert asked mathematicians to put all of mathematics into one formal axiom system and to prove, using only simple finite reasoning, that the system is consistent; he expected it also to be complete, so that every true statement could be derived.

title: Ludwig Wittgenstein
summary: Austrian philosopher. His early work tried to define exactly what can be said in a logical language; his later work argued that meaning comes from how language is used in life.

title: Ludwig Wittgenstein
summary: A short, austere book claiming that the world is the totality of facts, that language mirrors facts through logical form, and that what can be said at all can be said clearly, and what cannot be spoken of must be passed over in silence. Wittgenstein wrote it largely in the trenches of the First World War and later rejected much of it.

title: Ludwig Wittgenstein
summary: Wittgenstein's later work, which abandons the idea of one exact logical language. Meaning comes from how words are used in many overlapping 'language games'.

title: Freud and psychoanalysis
summary: Freud pictured the mind as three agencies: the id (drives), the ego (the self that negotiates with reality) and the superego (internalised rules). Psychoanalysis interprets behaviour as the outcome of their conflicts.

title: Qualia
summary: The 'what it is like' qualities of experience: the redness of red, the painfulness of pain. Many philosophers think they resist physical explanation.

title: Qualia
summary: The 'Mary' argument. A scientist who knows all the physical facts about colour but has never seen colour seems to learn something new when she first sees red, which Jackson took to show that physical facts are not all the facts.

title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
summary: Gödel proved that any consistent formal system rich enough to do arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency. He did it by encoding statements about the system as numbers inside the system.

title: Alfred Tarski
summary: Polish logician who gave the standard formal definition of truth for logical languages and put semantics on a rigorous footing.

title: Alan Turing and computability
summary: English mathematician who defined computation with his abstract machine, helped found AI with the 1950 imitation-game paper, and late in life modelled how chemical patterns form in biology. During the Second World War he led the Bletchley Park section that broke German naval Enigma and designed the Bombe machine used to do it.

title: Alan Turing and computability
summary: Everything that can be effectively computed can be computed by a Turing machine, so all sufficiently powerful computers are equivalent in what they can compute. It is a thesis rather than a theorem, because 'effectively computable' is an informal notion.

title: Alan Turing and computability
summary: An imaginary device with a tape, a read-write head and a table of rules. Despite its simplicity it can carry out any calculation that any computer can, which makes it the standard definition of computation.

title: Alan Turing and computability
summary: Turing showed that no general procedure can decide, for every program, whether it will eventually stop or run forever. Some well-posed questions therefore have no computable answer.

title: Alan Turing and computability
summary: A model of computation proposed by Emil Post in the same year as Turing's, built from very simple instructions on a tape of marked and unmarked boxes.

facet: Computing Machinery and Intelligence (the Turing test)
title: Alan Turing and computability
summary: The paper that asks 'Can machines think?' and replaces the question with an imitation game, later called the Turing test: if a machine can hold a conversation indistinguishable from a human's, we should grant it intelligence. It also answers a list of objections, including one from telepathy.

title: Lambda calculus and combinators
summary: Different formal definitions of what it means to compute (Turing's machines, Church's lambda calculus, Schönfinkel's combinators) turned out to be equivalent. The Church-Turing thesis says they capture everything that can be computed at all.

title: Lambda calculus and combinators
summary: Logician who invented combinatory logic, showing that all functions can be built from a couple of basic combinators, a precursor of the lambda calculus and functional programming.

title: Behaviorism
summary: The school that restricted psychology to observable behaviour and treated talk of inner mental representations as unscientific. Skinner explained behaviour through its consequences: actions that are reinforced become more frequent.

title: Maslow: A Theory of Human Motivation
summary: Maslow's ranking of human needs, from bodily needs up to self-fulfilment.

title: McCulloch–Pitts neurons
summary: McCulloch and Pitts showed in 1943 that networks of simple threshold units can compute logical functions. In 1986 Rumelhart and McClelland's 'Parallel Distributed Processing' revived neural networks as models of cognition.

title: Schrödinger: life as negentropy
summary: In 'What is Life?' Schrödinger suggested that organisms stay ordered by feeding on 'negative entropy': they export disorder to their environment.

title: John von Neumann and the first computers
summary: Hungarian-American polymath who shaped game theory, quantum mechanics and the stored-program computer architecture that bears his name. He also designed self-reproducing automata, an early formal model of life.

title: John von Neumann and the first computers
summary: Babbage designed a mechanical general-purpose computer in the 1830s; Zuse built the first working programmable computers in Germany around 1941; von Neumann defined the stored-program architecture still used today.

title: John von Neumann and the first computers
summary: Showed how to build reliable computation out of noisy, failure-prone parts by using redundancy.

title: Claude Shannon and information theory
summary: Shannon defined information as reduction of uncertainty, measurable in bits, and showed how much of it can be sent over a noisy channel.

title: Claude Shannon and information theory
summary: Shannon's paper 'Programming a Computer for Playing Chess' distinguished between searching all moves to a fixed depth and selectively exploring promising lines.

title: Cybernetics
summary: The mid-century science of control and feedback in animals and machines, which grew out of control engineering and fed into systems theory and neural networks. Norbert Wiener named it in 1948; its core idea is that purposeful behaviour comes from feedback loops.

title: Cybernetics
summary: Under President Allende, Chile tried to steer its nationalised economy in real time using telex data, computer models and a futuristic operations room. The 1973 coup ended it.

title: Materialism and physicalism
summary: The thesis that everything that exists is physical or depends on the physical, with no extra mental or supernatural ingredients. It is the default position in most of contemporary science and analytic philosophy.

title: Materialism and physicalism
summary: The philosophical position that we perceive the world itself, roughly as it is, rather than an internal representation of it.

title: Turing's morphogenesis
summary: Turing showed that interacting chemicals that diffuse at different rates spontaneously form spots and stripes. Neural cellular automata are a modern descendant: grids of identical cells that learn local rules to grow and repair a pattern.

title: Developmental stage theories
summary: Theories that describe mental growth as a series of stages: Piaget for children's thinking, Loevinger for ego development, Kohlberg for moral reasoning.

title: The Doors of Perception
summary: Huxley's report of taking mescaline, in which he suggests the brain normally filters a much wider field of awareness.

title: The founding of AI
summary: The 1956 summer meeting at Dartmouth College where the term 'artificial intelligence' was adopted and the field was founded on the bet that every aspect of intelligence can be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it.

title: The founding of AI
summary: Computer scientist who coined the term 'artificial intelligence', organised the 1956 Dartmouth workshop and invented Lisp. He championed formal logic as the language in which machines should represent knowledge.

title: Cortical columns
summary: The neocortex appears to be built from repeating vertical circuits: minicolumns of about a hundred neurons, bundled into larger columns. Mountcastle proposed that these columns are the cortex's basic, general-purpose computing unit.

title: Many-worlds interpretation
summary: The reading of quantum mechanics in which the wave function never collapses; every possible outcome happens in a separate branch of the universe. Hugh Everett proposed it in 1957; observers split along with everything else, so each copy sees a single outcome.

title: Marvin Minsky
summary: Co-founder of the field of artificial intelligence at MIT. In 'The Society of Mind' (1986) and 'The Emotion Machine' (2006) he described the mind as a large crowd of simple cooperating processes, with no single principle behind it.

title: Marvin Minsky
summary: Minsky's picture of the mind as a crowd of simple, mindless agents whose interactions add up to intelligence. The book is written as hundreds of one-page essays, each describing one piece of the machinery.

title: Marvin Minsky
summary: A mathematical analysis showing that single-layer neural networks cannot learn certain simple functions. It was widely read as proof that neural networks were a dead end, and funding dried up for over a decade.

title: Noam Chomsky
summary: Linguist who argued that language rests on an innate grammar faculty, and a long-standing sceptic that statistical models tell us anything about the mind. His work in the 1950s helped end behaviourism and start cognitive science.

title: Pandemonium model
summary: An early model of perception as a crowd of 'demons', each shouting when it detects its pattern, with higher demons listening for the loudest.

title: Functionalism and computationalism
summary: Functionalism says a mental state is defined by what it does, not what it is made of. Computationalism adds that what minds do can be described as computation.

title: Functionalism and computationalism
summary: Weak computationalism says minds are computer programs realised in brains. Strong computationalism (digital physics, pancomputationalism) adds that the universe itself is best described as computation that generates patterns of information.

title: Stanisław Lem
summary: Polish science fiction writer and philosopher of technology. 'Solaris' (1961) is about an alien mind humans cannot understand; 'Golem XIV' (1981) is a set of lectures given by a superhuman computer to humanity.

title: Stanisław Lem
summary: Novel about scientists orbiting a planet whose ocean is a single vast mind that they can never understand. Stanisław Lem wrote it in 1961; the ocean answers the scientists by materialising figures from their own memories.

title: Stanisław Lem
summary: Lem's non-fiction survey of future technologies, including artificial intelligence, virtual reality and directed evolution.

title: Solomonoff induction
summary: Inventor of algorithmic probability, a mathematically ideal (though uncomputable) theory of learning by preferring the shortest programs that explain the data. He attended the 1956 Dartmouth workshop and his ideas underlie later formal theories of universal intelligence.

title: Alexey Ivakhnenko
summary: Soviet-Ukrainian mathematician who trained multi-layer networks in the 1960s (the Group Method of Data Handling), often cited as the earliest deep learning.

title: Symbolic AI
summary: The first paradigm of AI: represent knowledge as symbols and logical rules and reason over them. Expert systems encoded specialists' rules by hand.

title: Symbolic AI
summary: Carnegie Mellon pair who wrote the first AI programs and proposed that intelligence is the manipulation of physical symbols. Their 'physical symbol system hypothesis' was the working creed of classical AI.

title: ELIZA
summary: An early chat program that imitated a therapist using simple pattern matching. Many users felt understood by it.

title: Timothy Leary and the eight-circuit model
summary: A counter-culture model that describes eight 'circuits' of the nervous system, from basic survival up to mystical states.
